newsitem.title: UK: ATHLETICS-PINTO SETS SIGHTS ON ATHENS AFTER MARATHON WIN.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-PINTO SETS SIGHTS ON ATHENS AFTER MARATHON WIN.

text.p: Portugal's Antonio Pinto won the men's London marathon on Sunday and then set his sights on a world championship medal in August.

"I'll be definitely running in Athens. It's now very important to me to get a major championship medal to add to my resume," he said after one of the closest finishes in the history of the London marathon.
"I did not do well in either the Olympics or the European championships."

Pinto, who won here in 1992, notched up his third career victory in 10 outings over the marathon distance, beating Italy's Stefano Baldini by two seconds in a sprint finish. Olympic champion Josiah Thugwane of South Africa was third.
Pinto's time of two hours seven minutes 55 seconds was a course record but the Portuguese runner was far from certain for most of the race that he was going to come out on top.

"At about 30 kilometres I was thinking about finishing in the top three again. It was only at 40 kilometres that I started to think I could win. As we went further I got stronger, and started more and more to think that I could win."
By contrast, women's winner Joyce Chepchumba of Kenya believed throughout that she could win despite a close battle with home favourite and last year's champion Liz McColgan.

"I always felt confident, especially as the first 10 miles were quite easy," said Chepchumba. "The pace set by Lorna (Kiplagat) was very good. As far as the finish is concerned I knew Liz would try her best and so I also had to try my best."
Chepchumba won in a national record of 2:26:51 with McColgan just one second further back, reversing their positions of last year.
McColgan was far from happy with her effort despite a personal best, eclipsing the 2:27:32 she ran to win in New York on her debut over the distance six years ago.
"I feel very disappointed despite the time. I had stomach problems over the first half of the race and at 20 miles I did not even think I would be in the top five."
Pinto drew level with Baldini as they approached the finish as Thugwane, who had broken away after 22 miles (35 kms) began to flag.
"When Thugwane faded I knew I could beat Stefano in the last part of the race," said Pinto.
"Even though he outsprinted me in the Lisbon half marathon last month, the half marathon and the marathon are two very different races and I have got more experience at the longer race."
Baldini's national best leaves the Italian runner with a dilemma over which event to tackle at the world championships.
He had originally planned to do the 10,000 metres but may now change his plans.
Thugwane was very pleased with his third place in 2:08:06 despite missing his national record by just two seconds.
He improved his personal best by three-and-a-half minutes.

"I came here on a mission because a lot of people, both in South Africa and outside, thought I would never run a good race again after Atlanta. I have now proved them all wrong," said the Olympic champion.
